bipartite.note: Dickens radically transforms the poem: he reverses the speaker/addressee relationship, turning it into a male speaker reproaching a 'maiden' for not coming, rather than the original female speaker recalling the man's promise. The causal-physical logic (promise leads to the long vigil ending in the ariake moon) is inverted into a direct reproach ('why com'st thou not'), and the shimo's moon description is repositioned as an accusatory backdrop rather than the emblem of a completed, bitter vigil. The temporal unfolding (waiting through the night until dawn) collapses into a static rebuke scene.

kakekotoba_handling.note: Dickens renders 長月 (Nagatsuki, the ninth month) as 'long-moon,' a mistranslation that conflates 長月 with 有明の月 by pulling the 'naga' (long) association forward and fusing it with 'moon' rather than 'month.' This captures the secondary/associative resonance of 'long' (long night, long wait) but discards the primary calendrical meaning of the ninth month entirely, and invents a compound 'long-moon' that doesn't exist in the source's semantics — it is a transformed rendering rather than a clean primary/secondary split.

kigo_handling.note: The autumn month name 長月 is replaced by the invented phrase 'long-moon night,' which relocates the 'long' association from the calendar month to the moon itself, producing a seasonal marker that reads as an odd proper-noun-like descriptor rather than conveying the classical autumn atmosphere of a nine-month lunar dusk. No autumn imagery (cold, dew, insects, foliage) is added to compensate, so the season's felt atmosphere is largely lost even though the phrase gestures at 'long' night.

entries.content_summary: Address to a 'maiden' scolding her for being heedless of her vow — inverts the source's implied situation where the male lover failed to come, recast as a female addressee failing her vow.
Question 'why com'st thou not' plus naming of 'long-moon night' (mistranslated 長月), compressing the causal setup and the month name together.
The Ariake moon shining now — direct rendering of 有明の月.

Description of the moon's light as 'forgetfulless' and welcoming, an interpretive elaboration of 待ち出でつるかな (the emergence of the moon after the long wait), reframed as the moon's steadfast/welcoming quality rather than the speaker's bitter vigil.

line_mapping.structural_note: Dickens compresses the jokotoba (今来むといひしばかりに) into a two-line rhetorical question addressed to a 'maiden,' inverting gender roles from the original (traditionally read as a woman's lament over a man's broken promise) into a man's reproach of a woman; the shimo-no-ku's emotional pivot (the moon as sole witness to the failed wait) becomes instead a description of the moon's benevolent light, losing the irony of the original pivot.

Dickens.translator_strategy: Dickens prioritizes a rhyming, quatrain-form English lyric with an invented address to a 'maiden,' sacrificing the source's gender voicing, the precise calendrical kakekotoba, and the bitter irony of the ariake moon pivot in favor of a smooth, moralizing reproach poem.

bipartite.note: The translation reorders the poem so that the waiting-for-the-moon image (shimo content) appears first (L1-L2) and the lover's broken promise (kami content) appears last (L3-L4), reversing the causal-physical sequence of the original where the promise precedes and motivates the long wait. The causal logic is still present in a loose sense—the reader can infer the promise explains the wait—but syntactically the effect-then-cause order inverts the original's cause-then-effect structure, and the exclamation-mark ending on the promise reframes it as bitter realization rather than initial premise.

kakekotoba_handling.note: Noguchi transliterates 長月 as 'Naga Tsuki' (treating it almost as a proper name/moon-title fused with 'morning moon'), preserving the calendrical/primary reading as a proper noun but losing entirely the resonance with 'long' (nagai) that reinforces the long-night waiting motif; ironically 'naga' is present in the romanization but not conveyed as meaning 'long' to an English reader, so the secondary suggestive resonance is not functionally translated.

kigo_handling.note: The literal month-name is transliterated but not translated or explained as 'ninth month/autumn'; no autumnal atmosphere (cold, long night, falling leaves) is evoked elsewhere in the translation, so the seasonal signal is present only as an opaque proper noun to non-Japanese readers and functionally omitted as a kigo.

entries.content_summary: 'Now I have to wait' — renders the shimo-no-ku's waiting motif, displaced to the opening line
'Only for the Naga Tsuki morning moon to appear' — combines 長月 (transliterated) with 有明の月 ('morning moon'), compressing ku 3 and 4 into one line
'But thy word of promise' — renders いひしばかりに, the promise/speech act of the kami-no-ku, now placed after the waiting instead of before it
'To come and see me soon!' — renders 今来むと, the lover's actual promised words, placed last for emphatic/ironic effect

line_mapping.structural_note: The translator inverts the temporal/logical sequence of the original: instead of promise-then-wait (kami then shimo), the English gives wait-then-promise, turning the poem into something closer to a retrospective lament ending on the broken words themselves, with 'soon' ironically undercutting 'now' (ima) and the exclamation point turning the final line into an outcry rather than a simple report.

Noguchi.translator_strategy: Noguchi prioritizes a compact, rhyme-adjacent English quatrain that foregrounds the emotional irony of the broken promise by reversing chronological order, sacrificing the seasonal/kakekotoba nuance of 長月 and the causal kami-shimo sequence for lyrical compression and an exclamatory closing line.

bipartite.note: Porter reorders the poem so the shimo-no-ku content (the ariake moon witnessed after a night's wait) opens the translation (L1-L2), while the kami-no-ku content (the lover's promise 'ima kon') is placed at the end (L3-L5). This reverses the causal-physical sequence: source moves promise→wait→moon, but Porter moves moon→wait→promise, effectively inverting cause and effect into a retrospective structure where the moon is seen first and the promise is recalled afterward as explanation.

kakekotoba_handling.note: Porter translates 長月 simply as 'autumn' (via 'autumn morn'), losing both the specific calendrical name Nagatsuki and the なが/'long' resonance with the long night of waiting; no attempt to capture the 'long' undertone survives explicitly, though 'the whole night through' in L1 does gesture at duration, it is decoupled from the 長月 word itself.

kigo_handling.note: The season is named outright as 'autumn' rather than through pure imagery, a fairly direct explicit rendering, though it loses the specific poetic month-name Nagatsuki and its 'long' connotation; the moon-through-the-night imagery in L1 reinforces the autumn dawn atmosphere.

entries.content_summary: The moon that shone the whole night through — refers to the ariake moon witnessed at dawn after the long wait, front-loaded from shimo-no-ku
'This autumn morn I see' — combines the autumn season marker (長月) with the moment of seeing the moon (有明の月を...出でつるかな)
'As here I wait thy well-known step' — recasts the waiting (待ち出でつる) as waiting for footsteps, adding a physical detail not explicit in source
'For thou didst promise me' — the lover's promise, corresponding to いひしばかりに
Direct quotation 'I'll surely come to thee' rendering 今来むと as reported speech

line_mapping.structural_note: Porter inverts the chronological order of the poem: the moon/wait (shimo) is presented first, followed by the promise (kami) as explanatory flashback, and expands the single word 待ち into a scene of listening for footsteps, plus renders 今来むと as a full direct quotation at poem's end for emotional emphasis.

Porter.translator_strategy: Porter prioritizes a natural, chronologically inverted English narrative (moon first, promise as explanatory close) and singable rhyme/meter over preserving the source's kami-shimo sequence or its subtle morphological wordplay.

bipartite.note: The translation preserves the causal-physical logic: the promise ('I will come') in L1-2 directly motivates the waiting described in L3-5, culminating in the appearance of the dawn moon. The word 'awaited' in L3 acts as the pivot linking the broken promise to the emblematic moon, matching the source's causal structure.

kakekotoba.note: McCauley translates 長月 (Nagatsuki) literally as 'the long month,' which actually captures both the calendrical name's etymology and the resonance with 'long' waiting — but only by literalizing the etymology rather than preserving a genuine double meaning as a live pivot. Since 'long' is explicitly stated, it reads as a gloss on the month name rather than a wordplay; the secondary emotional resonance (long night of waiting) is present but flattened into direct statement rather than functioning as a subtle undertone, so this counts as primary_only with the 'long' sense made explicit rather than pivoting.

kigo.note: McCauley renders 長月 literally as 'the long month,' which is not the conventional English name for autumn but does gesture toward the calendrical/seasonal marker; combined with 'moon of dawn' it evokes the long autumn night atmosphere, though the season 'autumn' itself is never named outright, making this more implicit than fully explicit — however since 'long month' is a direct calque of the actual seasonal term, it functions as an explicit (if opaque to non-specialist readers) naming of the kigo.

entries.content_summary: Just because she said — sets up the jokotoba premise
'In a moment I will come' — the lover's promise quoted
I've awaited her — the waiting motif, compressing 待ち出でつる's action into present perfect
E'en until the moon of dawn — 有明の月, the ariake moon
In the long month, hath appeared — 長月, placed out of original ku order, completing the verb 'appeared' for 出でつる

line_mapping.structural_note: McCauley inverts the ku-3 (長月) and ku-4 (有明の月) content, placing 'the long month' after 'the moon of dawn' rather than before, likely for rhyme/meter; also splits the waiting verb (待ち出でつる) across L3 and L5, with 'awaited' in L3 anticipating the object completed by 'hath appeared' in L5.

McCauley.translator_strategy: McCauley prioritizes literal, word-for-word fidelity to the Japanese syntax and vocabulary (including a literal calque of 長月 as 'the long month') even at the cost of natural English word order and rhyme-driven inversion of ku-3 and ku-4 content.
